So imagine there is an asteroid or whatever in trajectory to Earth at almost the speed of light. Is it possible to detect it before hitting the Earth?

The problem is, if the object is traveling at the speed of light, wouldn't the information take the same amount of time as the physical object to arrive thus detecting it just before the impact?
Can we see something coming to us at almost the speed of light?

Well, luckily things don't go the speed of light. Objects don't at least.

If something were going at nearly the speed of light, you would see its afterimage. An afterimage is you continuing to see something after the original thing is gone. But the afterimage of such a fast moving object would be a blur to us, like how we don't see individual bits of light.

A near-to-light-speed object moving along would be impossible for a person to track without a lot of sciency goodness on hand. We'd need to know where it was a good distance away.

As we found the object, learned the path it was going, and how fast it was moving we could then come up with an educated guess as to where it actually was and therefore its future path.

There is a lot of sky out there to look at, so the odds are if we were to have such an object on a path to hit us, we'd never know until after it happened.
